nodes.title: What “rational” means
nodes.summary: a/b is rational for every integer a.
assumptions: b is a nonzero integer.
nodes.conclusion: a/b is rational for every integer a.
nodes.justification: This is the definition of ℚ; equality identifies fractions a/b and c/d when ad=bc. It is a definition, not a theorem about a particular constant.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Integer arithmetic rules
nodes.summary: Sums, products and negatives are integers; products of nonzero integers are nonzero.
assumptions: a,b,c are integers.
nodes.conclusion: Sums, products and negatives are integers; products of nonzero integers are nonzero.
nodes.justification: These elementary integer facts are accepted at this boundary. A construction from natural numbers would need the corresponding induction and order arguments.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Why adding rationals stays rational
assumptions: x=a/b and y=c/d with integer a,b,c,d and b,d≠0.
nodes.justification: Integer arithmetic puts ad+bc and bd in ℤ and bd≠0. The displayed fraction therefore satisfies the definition of rational.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Why multiplying rationals stays rational
assumptions: x=a/b and y=c/d with integer a,b,c,d and b,d≠0.
nodes.justification: The numerators are integers; the denominators remain nonzero. Apply the definition of ℚ.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: The induction principle
assumptions: P(n) is a proposition about positive integers.
nodes.justification: Induction is a foundational principle of the natural numbers. It cannot be replaced by checking finitely many examples.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Why any finite sum or product of rationals is rational
nodes.summary: Their sum and product are rational.
assumptions: There are finitely many rational terms.
nodes.conclusion: Their sum and product are rational.
nodes.justification: For one term this is immediate. Adding or multiplying one more rational preserves rationality by the two closure lemmas. Induction handles any positive number of terms. The empty sum 0 and empty product 1 are rational by definition.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Determinant as a finite signed sum
nodes.summary: det A=Σσ sign(σ)∏ᵢAᵢ,σ(i), over permutations σ of {1,…,n}.
assumptions: A is an n×n matrix and n≥1.
nodes.conclusion: det A=Σσ sign(σ)∏ᵢAᵢ,σ(i), over permutations σ of {1,…,n}.
nodes.justification: This Leibniz formula can be used to define the determinant. There are finitely many permutations and every sign is +1 or −1.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Why rational matrix entries give a rational determinant
assumptions: Every entry of a finite square matrix A is rational.
nodes.justification: Each product in the determinant formula is rational. Multiplying by its integer sign preserves rationality, and the finite sum remains rational. No invertibility assumption is needed: zero determinants are rational too.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Unique prime factorization of a rational
nodes.summary: q=±∏p p^eₚ, with integer eₚ and finite support.
assumptions: q is a nonzero rational.
nodes.conclusion: q=±∏p p^eₚ, with integer eₚ and finite support.
nodes.justification: Factor the nonzero numerator and denominator into primes and subtract their exponents. This uses the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, whose proof is not expanded here.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Define a prime valuation and prime absolute value
assumptions: q≠0 is rational and p is prime.
nodes.justification: Here eₚ is the exponent in the prime factorization. If valuation is extended to zero, use v_p(0)=+∞; |0|_p=0. The nonzero product formula does not apply to zero.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Cancel matching prime powers
assumptions: Only finitely many integers eₚ are nonzero.
nodes.justification: Because the products are finite, regroup each p^eₚ with p^(−eₚ). Each pair equals p⁰=1. There is no interchange of an infinite product or limit.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Derive the rational product formula
assumptions: q is a nonzero rational.
nodes.justification: Prime factorization gives |q|∞=∏p p^eₚ; the prime absolute values give the reciprocal factors. Finite cancellation proves the identity. Estimating individual factors for a research construction is a separate task.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: A finite valuation implies nonzero
assumptions: v_p(q) is defined with v_p(0)=+∞.
v_p(q) is finite.
nodes.justification: If q=0, its valuation would be +∞ by definition, contradicting the finite value. This implication does not prove that a particular determinant has a finite valuation.

assumptions: Assume G is rational.
Use the manuscript construction for sufficiently large primes p.

nodes.title: Split the source nonvanishing claim
nodes.summary: Δ_p≠0 for sufficiently large primes p.
assumptions: Assume all hypotheses and the valuation conclusion of the source proposition.
nodes.conclusion: Δ_p≠0 for sufficiently large primes p.
nodes.justification: For each such p, −96p is finite. The elementary finite-valuation lemma then gives nonvanishing. This splits a difficult valuation estimate from an easy logical consequence; it does not eliminate the difficult estimate.

nodes.title: Finite sums can be distributed and reordered
assumptions: Work over a field; all sums here are finite.
nodes.justification: Associativity, commutativity of addition, and distributivity justify these finite identities by induction on the number of summands. No claim about infinite-series reordering is being used.

nodes.title: Coordinates define a matrix action
assumptions: A is m×k and y is a k-component vector.
nodes.justification: A matrix represents a linear map relative to chosen bases; the coordinate action is this finite sum.

nodes.title: Expand two successive matrix actions
assumptions: A is m×k, B is k×n, and x has n components.
nodes.justification: First use the matrix-action definition on A and y=Bx. Then replace yₗ by ΣⱼBₗⱼxⱼ and distribute Aᵢₗ across that finite sum.

nodes.title: Identify the matrix of a composition
assumptions: A is m×k, B is k×n, and x has n components.
nodes.justification: Reorder the finite double sum to group each coefficient of xⱼ: Σⱼ(ΣₗAᵢₗBₗⱼ)xⱼ. By the matrix-action definition this is Cx. This explains the multiplication formula; it says nothing about optimal algorithmic complexity.

nodes.title: The multivariable chain rule
assumptions: u and the curve γ are continuously differentiable on the relevant domain.
nodes.justification: This is an accepted calculus theorem at the current boundary. A proof proceeds from differentiability’s linear approximation and a remainder tending to zero. That remainder proof is not expanded here.

nodes.title: Zero derivative implies constant on an interval
assumptions: h is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and h′=0 there.
nodes.justification: The mean value theorem gives h(b)−h(a)=h′(c)(b−a)=0 for some c∈(a,b). The mean value theorem is expanded below.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Follow a straight characteristic
assumptions: u is C¹ and solves u_t+c u_x=0.
c is constant and x(t)=x₀+ct.
nodes.justification: The curve has x′(t)=c. Substitute into the chain rule and then into the assumed PDE. Its left side is exactly u_t+c u_x, which vanishes.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Recover the transport solution
assumptions: u is a C¹ solution of u_t+c u_x=0 with u(0,x)=u₀(x).
Characteristic segments lie in the solution domain.
nodes.justification: The previous step makes u constant along each characteristic, so u(t,x₀+ct)=u₀(x₀). Set x₀=x−ct. Conversely, for C¹ u₀, differentiating u₀(x−ct) checks the PDE and initial value. This handles constant-speed transport, not the full nonlinear coupled system.

nodes.title: Product and exponential differentiation
assumptions: f,g are differentiable, and C is constant.
nodes.justification: Combine the product-rule derivation with the separately stated exponential derivative. The exponential fact remains an explicit boundary.

nodes.title: Nonpositive derivative gives a nonincreasing function
assumptions: F is continuous on [0,T], differentiable on (0,T), and F′≤0.
nodes.justification: For t>0, the mean value theorem gives F(t)−F(0)=tF′(c)≤0. Equality at t=0 is immediate. Follow the mean-value node for its derivation.

nodes.title: Remove exponential growth by a weight
assumptions: E is differentiable and E′≤CE; C is constant.
nodes.justification: Product differentiation gives F′=e^(−Ct)(E′−CE). The assumed inequality makes the bracket nonpositive; the exponential is positive, so multiplying preserves its sign.

nodes.title: Derive a basic Grönwall bound
assumptions: E is continuous on [0,T], differentiable on (0,T), and E′≤CE.
C is a fixed real constant.
nodes.justification: The weighted quantity F is nonincreasing, hence e^(−Ct)E(t)≤E(0). Multiply by positive e^(Ct). The bound is conditional on an established differential inequality; deriving one for a research PDE is separate work.

nodes.summary: An improved exponent needs a valid construction and a justified complexity bound.
assumptions: Use the exact algorithmic model and constructions of the manuscript.
nodes.conclusion: An improved exponent needs a valid construction and a justified complexity bound.
nodes.justification: The coordinate identity proves what multiplication computes. It does not construct a faster algorithm. Tensor decompositions, their validity over the specified field, and their asymptotic analysis remain unexpanded research work.

nodes.summary: Global smoothness needs a valid continuation argument with sufficiently strong a priori control.
assumptions: Use the actual nonlinear Vlasov–Maxwell system and its initial-data assumptions.
nodes.conclusion: Global smoothness needs a valid continuation argument with sufficiently strong a priori control.
nodes.justification: A free-transport solution or a generic Grönwall lemma does not supply those estimates. The actual force bounds, regularity requirements, and continuation theorem must be checked in the manuscript. This boundary marks missing work rather than a proved implication.

nodes.title: Derivative as a first-order approximation
assumptions: f is differentiable at a.
nodes.justification: Rewrite the derivative limit by defining r(h)=f(a+h)−f(a)−f′(a)h. The defining difference quotient says exactly that r(h)/h tends to zero. Set r(0)=0.

nodes.title: Arithmetic of limits and differentiability
nodes.summary: Limits preserve finite sums and products; differentiability implies continuity.
assumptions: All named limits exist as finite real numbers.
nodes.conclusion: Limits preserve finite sums and products; differentiability implies continuity.
nodes.justification: These real-analysis results are accepted at this boundary. They follow from epsilon-delta estimates. Their hypotheses exclude expressions such as an undefined infinity times zero.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Derive the product rule
assumptions: f and g are differentiable at a.
nodes.justification: For h≠0, write [f(a+h)g(a+h)−f(a)g(a)]/h as ([f(a+h)−f(a)]/h)g(a+h)+f(a)([g(a+h)−g(a)]/h). Take limits, using g(a+h)→g(a).
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Derivative and positivity of the exponential
assumptions: t and C are real; C is constant.
nodes.justification: This standard exponential-function fact remains a boundary. A derivation depends on how exp is defined, for example by a power series or as an inverse of an integral-defined logarithm.

nodes.title: Extreme-value theorem on a closed interval
nodes.summary: h attains both its maximum and minimum on [a,b].
assumptions: h is continuous on a finite closed interval [a,b].
nodes.conclusion: h attains both its maximum and minimum on [a,b].
nodes.justification: This is a completeness-based theorem of real analysis. It is not implied by differentiability rules alone. Compactness of [a,b] is one route to its proof, left as the next explicit boundary.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Derivative at an interior extremum
assumptions: h is differentiable at an interior local maximum c.
nodes.justification: For small positive t, [h(c+t)−h(c)]/t≤0; for small negative t the quotient is ≥0. Since both sides tend to the same derivative, it is both ≤0 and ≥0, hence zero. At a local minimum reverse the signs.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Rolle’s theorem
assumptions: h is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), a<b, and h(a)=h(b).
nodes.justification: If h is constant, every interior derivative is zero. Otherwise some value differs from the common endpoint value. A maximum or minimum attained by the extreme-value theorem must then occur in the interior. The stationary-extremum result gives zero derivative there.
nodes.extraction: Curated logical decomposition. All outgoing Requires result premises are needed together. Definitions and unexpanded theorem or research boundaries are labeled explicitly.

nodes.title: Derive the mean value theorem
assumptions: h is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and a<b.
nodes.justification: Set m=(h(b)−h(a))/(b−a) and g(x)=h(x)−m(x−a). The endpoints of g agree. Rolle gives g′(c)=0, hence h′(c)=m. Multiply by b−a. Differentiation of the linear term follows directly from the derivative definition.
